cues.text: An Emperor's First Church Council
Barely a year after the Edict of Milan had granted Christianity legal toleration, Emperor Constantine summoned bishops from across the Western Empire, from Africa to Britain.
They gathered at Arles in southern Gaul in August 314, the first general council of the Western Church and the first ever convened at an emperor's own initiative.

Roughly thirty-three to forty-three bishops or their representatives attended, presided over by Marinus, bishop of the host city, with Pope Sylvester I, too occupied with affairs in Rome to travel himself, represented by legates.
The Donatist Dispute
The council's immediate purpose was to resolve the bitter Donatist controversy then dividing the North African Church.
Donatist Christians had rejected Caecilian's election as Bishop of Carthage in 311.
They argued that one ordaining bishop was a traditor — a Christian who had handed over sacred texts to be burned during the recent persecution — making his ordination invalid.

A council held at Rome in 313 had already ruled in Caecilian's favor, but the Donatists, unsatisfied, appealed directly to Constantine himself, prompting the emperor to convene a still larger and more representative assembly at Arles.
Vindicating Caecilian
The bishops at Arles upheld Caecilian's election, ruling that ordination performed by three bishops was canonically valid regardless of any bishop's personal worthiness.

The mere presence of a traditor among the consecrating bishops did not, by itself, invalidate the sacrament—a position rejecting the Donatist claim that a minister's moral state could nullify what he confected.
The council also explicitly condemned the Donatist practice of rebaptizing Catholics who joined their movement, insisting that baptism validly conferred could never be repeated.
Twenty-Two Canons for a Church at Peace
Beyond the Donatist question, Arles issued twenty-two disciplinary canons addressing the practical needs of a Church suddenly emerging into public legal existence.
It fixed a single, universal date for Easter and forbade clergy from abandoning their ordained churches.

It also excluded from communion Christian soldiers deserting their post in peacetime and Christian charioteers continuing in the public games—evidence of a Church defining ordinary Christian life after persecution ended.
Legacy
The Donatists rejected the council's ruling and appealed once more to Constantine personally, who upheld Arles's judgment.

The Donatist schism persisted in North Africa for centuries afterward, eventually requiring St. Augustine of Hippo's sustained theological and pastoral engagement two generations later to fully confront it.
St. Augustine himself later described Arles in terms suggesting something close to universal authority.
The council is remembered as the crucial dress rehearsal, in both form and imperial initiative, for the far larger ecumenical council Constantine would convene at Nicaea barely a decade afterward.
